clue.text: He passes out at the back of the pack

definitions.text: He passes out at the back of the pack

parts.words: He passes out at the back of the pack
parts.note: reads like someone fainting behind a crowd, but in rugby union the player behind the forwards' scrum feeds the ball out to the backs

explanation.walkthrough: 'passes out' suggests fainting; in rugby it means passing the ball out from the scrum, and 'the pack' is the eight forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union this player stands behind the scrum and passes the ball out to the backs.

clue.text: Vehicle reverses on rough ascent — what's the matter?

indicators.note: the vehicle's name is read backwards, as a vehicle reversing goes back

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle

indicators.note: rough here means roughly made, so the letters of ascent are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's wrong as a vehicle backs down a rough slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' turns BUS into SUB; 'rough' rearranges ASCENT into STANCE. 'What's the matter?' reads as a worried question but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Matter and substance are synonyms for physical material.

explanation.surface: Cash is levied somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' looks like a fee being levied but describes the animal's charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino is old British slang for cash; the animal is famous for charging on the African plains.

indicators.note: the letters are put back in a new order, replaced in other places

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a woman called Lea might stand in for a stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might' does double service in the surface only; in the parse 'Lea might' is the fodder and 'replace' the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A megalith is a great standing stone of prehistoric monuments.

clue.text: A tedious fellow holds I.T.V. variety is unsuccessful

indicators.note: the tedious fellow's word contains the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: a bore is a tedious person

indicators.note: a variety of the letters, so they are rearranged

parts.note: Independent Television, the British commercial channel

explanation.surface: A dull man presents ITV variety shows, which flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' looks like a television genre, but it is the anagram signal; 'holds' is the containment signal. ITV is Britain's commercial television channel.
explanation.definitionFit: An abortive attempt is one that fails, coming to nothing.

indicators.note: the saint's name as spoken gives letters spelt differently

parts.note: St Philip is one of the twelve apostles

explanation.surface: A saint's sermon gives people a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speech' signals a sound-alike: the name of St Philip, said out loud, matches a word spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A fillip is a boost or stimulus that livens something up.

indicators.note: the works go inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
OPS is short for opera, works

explanation.surface: Woodwork displayed in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' looks like a verb but is the plural of op., the abbreviation for opus; 'in' is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A copse is a small wood or thicket.

explanation.surface: Old wrecks hailing from Stoke and its pottery towns.
explanation.walkthrough: The Potteries is the Stoke-on-Trent district of England famous for ceramics; the question mark admits that pots are being called people.
explanation.definitionFit: Old crocks are worn-out people; crocks are also earthenware pots, the product of the Potteries, the pottery towns of Staffordshire.

indicators.note: collected again, so the letters are gathered up in a new order

explanation.surface: A stroll is remembered in a poem set in the Forest of Arden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recollected' looks like remembering but signals the letters re-collected into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A promenade is a leisurely walk, or the seafront path for one.

annotationWithheld.why: Animal found in Africa—or China? (5) for ELAND: no parse explains 'or China?'; neither hidden word nor double definition fits, and a web search found no explanation

explanation.surface: A sailor is asked to pause and come round.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is a sailor, so 'Stop for Jack' means the nautical sense of halting a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors (Jack Tars) bring a ship to when they halt it head to wind; bringing someone round restores consciousness.

clue.text: Girl gives high sign to another

parts.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac, high in the heavens
Nora is another girl's name

explanation.surface: One girl gives another a signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high sign' sounds like a signal, but it is a zodiac sign high in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonora is a woman's given name, as in Beethoven's heroine.

explanation.surface: Singing to the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To troll a song is to sing it heartily; to troll is also to fish by trailing a line behind a boat.

parts.note: broad-minded usually means tolerant; here it is read as a person whose head is thick and broad, a dolt

explanation.walkthrough: 'broad-minded' normally praises tolerance; here a broad head means a thick one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dolt is said to have a thick skull, so a dim person is called this.

explanation.surface: Someone denies any link with the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current affairs' suggests the news, but means electricity; 'connexion' is the old spelling of connection.
explanation.definitionFit: A refusal is a negative; a battery's minus terminal is its negative connection, which deals with electric current.

parts.note: seems to describe something threadbare, but means a garment worn outdoors, a heavy overcoat

explanation.walkthrough: 'worn out' suggests exhausted or threadbare; it means worn when going out.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy overcoat, as soldiers wore, is put on to go outdoors.

parts.note: pluckily seems to mean bravely, but describes an instrument played by plucking its strings

explanation.walkthrough: 'pluckily' would usually mean with courage; here it means by plucking.
explanation.definitionFit: This stringed instrument is sounded by plucking its strings with the fingers.

parts.note: range seems to mean literary scope, but is a kitchen stove; a hack work written just to keep the cooking pot boiling

explanation.walkthrough: 'range' suggests breadth of writing; it is a kitchen stove, on which a pot boils, and hack writing is done to keep the pot boiling.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack book written merely to earn a living is called this.

clue.text: Grey is to study Maugham's work

parts.note: ashen means grey, pale as ash
a den is a private study

explanation.surface: A pale writer settles down to study Somerset Maugham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grey' looks like a name or verb but is the colour; Ashenden is Maugham's book of spy stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashenden is W. Somerset Maugham's 1928 collection of stories about a British agent.

definitions.note: a noun phrase: the people sitting in court, judges or magistrates

parts.note: just means only
ices are light refreshments

explanation.surface: Only snacks are served in the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in court' reads as where the snacks are served but is the definition: those who sit in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges and magistrates sit on the bench in a court of law.

indicators.note: the answer is the run of letters contained within these words

explanation.surface: The furnishings of the seller's apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contents' looks like furniture and 'flat' an apartment; the letters inside 'the vendor's' give a word for level.
explanation.definitionFit: A level, smooth surface is flat.

indicators.note: the letters are wrongly placed, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive is read as a plural, tens

explanation.surface: A solver complains that clue ten is wrong, though it means something edible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges CLUE + TENS; the possessive 's counts as an S here.
explanation.definitionFit: Esculent is a formal word for edible, fit to be eaten.

explanation.surface: A dotted cape.
explanation.definitionFit: The pieces of the tile game are marked with spots; it is also a loose hooded cloak worn with a half-mask at masquerades.

explanation.surface: An artist alters course.
explanation.definitionFit: J.M.W. Turner was the English landscape painter; a person who turns, changing direction, is one too.

clue.text: Make known where dictator's food went ? That's about right !

indicators.note: the phrase for where the food went goes around the abbreviation for right

parts.note: into Il Duce, the title of Mussolini, the Italian dictator

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about where a dictator's meal ended up, answered approvingly.
explanation.walkthrough: The dictator's food went INTO DUCE (Mussolini was Il Duce); 'about' wraps that around R.
explanation.definitionFit: To introduce a person is to make them known to others.

clue.text: Thought Lancashire opener would be the best possible

parts.note: an idea is a thought

indicators.note: the opening letter of the county name, as a cricket opener begins the innings

explanation.surface: A thought that a Lancashire opening batsman would be perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' suggests a cricket opening batsman but takes the first letter of Lancashire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect, the best one could imagine, is ideal.

parts.note: sounds like a moment for a stroll outdoors, but means the speed at which a tune, an air, is taken in music

explanation.walkthrough: 'take the air' suggests going outside; in music an air is a tune, and this is the speed it is taken at.
explanation.definitionFit: In music this is the speed or pace of a piece.

annotationWithheld.why: Acted as Minehead half-back (5) for MIMED: no selection from MINEHEAD gives MIMED (MINE, HEAD and their reversals do not), so the parse cannot be shown; no reprint found

clue.text: No one book could bring back this feeling

indicators.note: the whole run of pieces is read backwards, brought back

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: No single book could revive this emotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bring back' turns the whole run of pieces around, not just the last; 'could' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a feeling such as joy or anger.

clue.text: The sort of system that is claimed to break down

indicators.note: the word claimed is broken down and its letters reassembled

explanation.surface: A system that its critics say is about to collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break down' looks like a system failing but rearranges 'claimed'.
explanation.definitionFit: The metric counting scheme based on tens is this sort of system.

clue.text: The game is to follow destiny

indicators.note: the word to comes after the word for destiny

parts.note: one's lot is one's fate or destiny

explanation.surface: Fatalism: the game is to go where destiny leads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is to follow destiny' reads as a motto; in the parse 'follow' only sets the order of the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: This numbers game is played with cards drawn by chance, like bingo.

clue.text: Fight fan calls with dire misgiving

parts.note: rings means telephone calls

indicators.note: the letters of dire are mis-given, set out wrongly in a new order

explanation.surface: A boxing fan phones round full of grim doubts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misgiving' looks like doubt but is the anagram signal; 'calls' means phone calls.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches boxing from seats beside the ring is a fight fan.
